source.title: Combinatorial properties of continuous graphs: A survey of challenges, solutions and open problems

accepted.question_text: Let Γ = (V, E) be a continuous graph in which each edge is a unit-length continuous interval, and let α_r(Γ) denote the maximum size of an r-independent set, meaning a set I ⊆ E such that every two distinct points p, q ∈ I satisfy d(p, q) ≥ 2r. The paper asks for a structural and complexity classification of this problem: as a function of both the radius r > 0 and the structure of the underlying graph, for which cases can one compute α_r(Γ) in polynomial time, and for which cases is the problem NP-hard?

evidence.quote: Definition 9. Given a positive real number r > 0, a set of points I ⊆ E is called an r-independent (or r-stable) set of Γ if for any two points p, q ∈ I, it holds that d(p, q) ≥ 2r. The r-independence number of Γ, further referred as αr(Γ) or αr for simplicity, is the cardinality of the maximum r-independent set in Γ.

Clearly, the complexity of the problem is highly dependent not only on the nature of the number r but also on the specific structure of the graph. Thus, the open question of this section is to have a picture of such a joint dependency.

accepted.question_text: For a continuous graph Γ, let α_1(Γ) be the maximum size of a 1-independent set in Γ, and let α(G(Γ)) be the size of a maximum independent set in the associated combinatorial graph G(Γ) on the same endpoints. The paper asks whether the ratio α_1(Γ(G)) / α(G) is always at most n/2 for an n-vertex graph, whether that bound is tight, and more generally how this ratio behaves for special graph classes and structural restrictions.
accepted.context_brief: relaxation gap for r=1 independent set

evidence.quote: It is unclear whether or not n/2 is a tight upper bound for the ratio α1(Γ(G))/α(G). We leave this as an open question of this section. Furthermore, we do expect that some structural properties of combinatorial graphs influence the ratio, and it is interesting to see how the ratio behaves in special cases/classes of graphs.

accepted.question_text: Let α_r(Γ) be the maximum size of an r-independent set in a continuous graph Γ, where an r-independent set is a subset I ⊆ E whose distinct points are pairwise at distance at least 2r. For a rational radius r > 0, does there exist a polynomial-time approximation algorithm for the maximum r-independent set problem whose approximation ratio is bounded below by an absolute constant that does not depend on the input size?

evidence.quote: Definition 9. Given a positive real number r > 0, a set of points I ⊆ E is called an r-independent (or r-stable) set of Γ if for any two points p, q ∈ I, it holds that d(p, q) ≥ 2r. The r-independence number of Γ, further referred as αr(Γ) or αr for simplicity, is the cardinality of the maximum r-independent set in Γ.

The specific open question we ask in this paragraph reads: For any rational number r > 0, is there a polynomial time approximation algorithm for the maximum r-independent set problem with performance guarantee bounded by a constant?

accepted.question_text: Let α_r(Γ) be the maximum size of an r-independent set in a continuous graph Γ, and let β_r(Γ) be the minimum number of radius-r balls needed to cover all points of Γ. For a continuous graph Γ with n endpoint vertices and a radius r > 0, what upper or lower bounds can one give for α_r(Γ) + β_r(Γ) as a function of n and r, and can such bounds be made tight?

evidence.quote: Definition 10. Given a positive real number r, a set of balls B = {B(p, r) : p ∈ E} is called an r-cover of Γ if for any point q ∈ E there is a ball B ∈ B containing q. The r-cover number of Γ is the cardinality of the minimum r-cover in Γ further denoted as βr(Γ) or βr for simplicity.
In general, the following question can be addressed: Given r > 0, what is the bound on αr(Γ) + βr(Γ) for a continuous graph Γ in terms of n and r? Is the bound tight?

accepted.question_text: For a combinatorial graph G, let β(G) be the size of a minimum vertex cover in G, and let β_1(Γ(G)) be the minimum number of radius-1 balls needed to cover the continuous graph Γ(G) obtained by replacing each edge of G by a unit-length interval. The paper asks for the largest possible value of the relaxation-gap ratio β(G) / β_1(Γ(G)) over all graphs G, with the conjecture that this ratio is at most 2.
accepted.context_brief: relaxation gap for r=1 vertex cover

evidence.quote: Similarly to the independent set problem above, the following natural open question arises: What is the highest ratio between β(G) and β1(Γ(G)) over all G? Following intuition from the matching theory and known results for the minimum vertex cover problem, we conjecture the ratio is at most 2.

accepted.question_text: Let β_r(Γ) denote the minimum cardinality of an r-cover of a continuous graph Γ, where an r-cover is a family of radius-r balls whose union contains every point of Γ. In the computationally hard cases where r is a non-unit rational fraction, what lower bounds can be proved for the approximation hardness of the minimum r-cover problem on continuous graphs?

evidence.quote: Definition 10. Given a positive real number r, a set of balls B = {B(p, r) : p ∈ E} is called an r-cover of Γ if for any point q ∈ E there is a ball B ∈ B containing q. The r-cover number of Γ is the cardinality of the minimum r-cover in Γ further denoted as βr(Γ) or βr for simplicity.

We suggest the following straightforward open question: For the hard cases of the problem (with the radius being a non-unit fraction, see Hartmann et al [16]), what are the lower bounds for the inapproximability of the minimum r-cover problem?

accepted.question_text: For the complete graph K_n, let Γ(K_n) be its continuous counterpart and let χ_{1/2}(Γ(K_n)) denote the minimum number of colors needed in a (1/2, c)-coloring, meaning a cover of Γ(K_n) by radius-1/2 balls together with a coloring of those balls such that intersecting balls receive different colors. What is the exact value of χ_{1/2}(Γ(K_n)) as a function of n? The paper conjectures that χ_{1/2}(Γ(K_n)) = ⌈n/2⌉.
accepted.context_brief: chromatic number of complete continuous graphs

evidence.quote: Definition 11. Graph Γ is (r, c)-colourable if there is a set of balls B = {B(p, r) : p ∈ E} forming an r-cover of Γ and an assignment f : B → {1, . . . , c} such that for every two balls B, B′ ∈ B having non-empty intersection, i.e. B ∩ B′ ≠ ∅, it holds that f(B) ≠ f(B′). The r-chromatic number of Γ, further denoted by χr(Γ) or χr for simplicity, is the minimum number of colours c such that Γ is (r, c)-colourable.
A seemingly simple question to ask is: What is the 1/2-chromatic number of Γ(Kn)? ... We conjecture that the 1/2-chromatic number of Γ(Kn) is ⌈n/2⌉.

accepted.question_text: Is every continuous planar graph (1/2, 3)-colourable? Equivalently, if Γ is a continuous graph that admits a planar embedding, must there always exist a cover of Γ by radius-1/2 balls that can be colored with three colors so that any two intersecting balls receive different colors? The paper also highlights the related lower-bound challenge of constructing a continuous planar graph that provably requires at least three colors.

evidence.quote: We conjecture that every continuous planar graph is (1/2, 3)-colourable. To get better intuition for this question, it would be helpful to find a continuous planar graph requiring at least 3 colours and to provide a formal proof of this lower bound of 3.

accepted.question_text: For a continuous graph Γ, let χ_{1/2}(Γ) be its radius-1/2 chromatic number. Does the strong inapproximability known for the ordinary chromatic number of combinatorial graphs also hold for χ_{1/2}(Γ) on continuous graphs? More concretely, does the same kind of hardness of approximation persist in the continuous setting?

evidence.quote: The question for the continuous version of the chromatic number problem remains as above: Whether or not the same hardness of approximation remains for the 1/2-chromatic number problem on continuous graphs?

accepted.question_text: Given a continuous graph Γ, can one bound its radius-1/2 chromatic number χ_{1/2}(Γ) above and below using the chromatic number χ(G(Γ)) of the associated combinatorial graph together with the number n of endpoint vertices? More broadly, can one derive useful upper and lower bounds for χ_{1/2}(Γ) from other graph parameters that are computable in polynomial time?

evidence.quote: Regardless computational complexity, an interesting question to address is: Given a continuous graph Γ, can one specify a lower and an upper bounds for χ1/2(Γ) in terms of a function of χ(G(Γ)) and n? Any other bounds for χ1/2 as functions of other (especially, polynomial-time computable) parameters are also very much interesting.

accepted.question_text: For a combinatorial graph G, define the treewidth of its continuous counterpart Γ(G) to be the 1-bramble number of Γ(G), where a 1-bramble is a family of subtrees of Γ(G) any two of which come within distance 1, and the order of the bramble is the minimum size of a point set hitting every subtree in the family. Is there a tractable algorithm that, given a continuous graph and a fixed small integer k > 0, decides whether its 1-bramble number is at most k?

evidence.quote: Definition 13. The treewidth of a continuous graph Γ(G) is the 1-bramble number of Γ(G).

On the other hand, recognizing whether the 1-bramble number of a continuous graph is at most k, for a given small integer k > 0, might be a very challenging and not necessarily tractable problem. We leave this as an open problem of this section.
